notesStmt.note: Whitman created this manuscript in late 1890 or early 1891. In With Walt Whitman in Camden, Horace Traubel writes that, on November 17, 1890, Whitman was "working on some poems" for Lippincott's, titled "'Old Age Echoes' or something like that." By December 19, most of the poems had been set in type, and Traubel conveyed to Whitman the editor's request for another poem to fill out a full page of the magazine. Whether the present manuscript was part of the first set or the poem Whitman wrote in response to this later request is unclear.

The poem here was published as "Sounds of the Winter" in the March 1891 issue of Lippincott's Magazine, along with three other poems under the corporate title "Old-Age Echoes." It later appeared in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891).

sourceDesc.bibl: med.00007.134 med.00007.166 Whitman, Walt Old Age Echoes 1890 or 1891 1792d850-c5d9-012f-7c66-58d385a7bc34 The Oscar Lion Papers, 1914–1955, New York Public Library, New York, N.Y. Transcribed from digital images of the original. The writing on the verso (not in Whitman's hand) makes reference to Good-Bye My Fancy and to "Sounds of Winter," as well as to a "Putnam 1902 Edition." There is also a postmark dated 18 October 1889, and a reference to Camden, New Jersey, that could be in Whitman's hand. The verso clearly displays the three separate pieces of paper that Whitman combined to draft "Old Age Echoes."

lg.head: Sounds of the Winter too.
lg.l: Sounds from of the winter too,

Sunshine upon the mountains—many a
distant strain

From cheery rail-road train‸—from nearer
field, barn, house,

The whisper'ding air—even the mute crops,
garner'd apples, corn,

Childrens' and women's tones—the rhythm of
farmer and of flail,

The old man's gay and garrulous
lips among the rest. Think not
we give it up yet give out yet.

Out of Forth from the snowy hairs we too
keep onup the lilt.
